papers.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
papers.abstract: Reliable robotic mapping in dynamic real-world environments is essential for embodied intelligence and long-term autonomy. However, existing methods often involve a trade-off: lightweight online mapping is efficient but captures limited semantic context, while dense mapping provides richer semantics at higher computational cost and is more vulnerable to distractors. They also struggle to relocalize objects after scene changes. To address these challenges, we propose the Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System (OASIS), a unified system for online mapping, complex open-vocabulary retrieval, and navigation in dynamic environments. Motivated by the observation that indoor scenes are organized around stable semantic anchors, OASIS represents the environment using a sparse set of anchor nodes, each maintaining a unified multimodal representation that integrates semantic descriptions, visual features, and geometric states for reasoning, verification, and navigation. Its compact anchor-centric memory supports on-demand evidence extraction and hierarchical retrieval, reducing redundant storage while improving retrieval reliability. To handle scene dynamics, OASIS further reuses transient observations collected during navigation to relocalize moved objects. Experiments in both simulation and real-world environments, including standard retrieval benchmarks and navigation tasks under both static and dynamic settings, demonstrate that our system can perform complex open-vocabulary retrieval and navigation, while also enabling relocation of displaced objects after scene changes.

papers.title: Know When to Escalate: Critic-Guided Adaptive Execution for Cloud-Local Embodied Agents
papers.abstract: Recent advances in foundation-model agents have enabled increasingly capable embodied systems for long-horizon planning and interaction. However, embodied agents require fast, closed-loop decisions as they continuously perceive and act on a changing environment. Deploying strong cloud agents leaves the platform idle for seconds between consecutive actions, while lightweight local models respond quickly but are more vulnerable to errors. Existing hierarchical architectures typically assign models fixed roles, whereas conventional model routers make stateless per-request decisions. We present CARE, a critic-guided adaptive execution framework that dynamically determines when to escalate control from a local executor to a stronger cloud model. A lightweight critic model monitors execution reliability and triggers escalation when local execution becomes unreliable; once escalated, control persists until the agent recovers, avoiding step-wise switching. To support such control transfer, a shared handoff memory maintains execution context and task-level progress across executors, enabling the model to intervene without restarting from scratch. Across diverse embodied benchmarks, CARE improves task success by 6.3-18.3 percentage points over the strongest evaluated collaboration baseline. CARE further approaches or exceeds Cloud-only success while reducing median time-between-action latency by 28.8-82.6%.

papers.title: Motion Retargeting with Spatiotemporal Preferences for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
papers.abstract: Human motion retargeting bridges the embodiment gap between humans and humanoid robots by converting human demonstrations into reference trajectories for whole-body control and loco-manipulation. For object-interaction tasks, successful execution depends on accurately preserving body--object relations at critical stages. However, uniform per-frame iteration budgets do not account for these localized accuracy requirements, limiting the computational efficiency of retargeting. To address this limitation, we present Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), which uses keyframes and key body parts to allocate optimization effort. Specifically, a vision-language model selects relevant motion signals and body parts, and keyframes are identified from changes in the selected signals. Based on these selections, STR assigns additional solver iterations to keyframes and higher interaction weights to the selected parts. To further improve contact fidelity, we introduce Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring (MCA) to refine object-surface contact positions using an approximate object-wrench model while retaining the selected surface directions. Building on the resulting references, we develop Spatiotemporal Reinforcement Learning (STRL), which combines adaptive key-stage sampling with a contact reward based on target proximity and object contact forces for downstream control. Simulation experiments on a Unitree G1 and real-world experiments on a Unitree R1 demonstrate that STR improves geometric contact coverage and continuity at lower computational cost, while the resulting references improve downstream task completion across diverse object-interaction motions.

papers.title: Decision Making and Ride Comfort Evaluation Based on Lane-Change Prediction for Autonomous Vehicles
papers.abstract: Predicting surrounding vehicles' lane-change intentions enables autonomous vehicles to anticipate potential hazards and respond proactively rather than relying solely on reactive maneuvers. This study investigates the benefits of integrating lane-change prediction, based on knowledge graph embeddings and Bayesian inference, into autonomous vehicle decision-making. Three driving strategies are evaluated in risky merging scenarios simulated in CARLA: reactive driving, prediction-based longitudinal action, and prediction-based lateral action. The proposed prediction model anticipates the surrounding vehicle's lane change approximately 3-4 seconds before its occurrence, allowing the ego vehicle to adjust its behavior accordingly. In the representative simulation records, reactive driving results in a collision accompanied by aggressive deceleration. In contrast, prediction-based longitudinal action initiates early braking to establish a safe gap, while prediction-based lateral action performs a lane change when a safe adjacent lane is available. Both predictive strategies avoid collisions in the evaluated records. Compared with reactive driving, peak deceleration before impact is reduced by 31.5% with longitudinal action and 91.0% with lateral action. Additionally, an ISO 2631-1-based horizontal vibration estimate is used to provide a ride comfort assessment. Overall, the results highlight the potential of lane-change prediction to support safer and smoother driving through proactive decision-making, with additional insights into ride comfort provided by vibration-based estimates.

papers.title: PhysibleMDM: Enforcing Inference-Time Physical Feasibility Constraints on Motion Diffusion Models via Noise Optimization
papers.abstract: Motion Diffusion Models (MDMs) can generate diverse and visually appealing human motion; yet, the resulting trajectories frequently violate physical constraints, limiting their downstream use in simulation and control. We present PhysibleMDM, a framework that promotes physical feasibility of MDM output by optimizing at inference time the diffusion noise without retraining the generative model. We introduce a set of surrogate feasibility constraints that can be evaluated without full trajectory simulation. These constraints combine kinematic checks (e.g., ground penetration, slip, and self-collision) with dynamic feasibility tests computed via an inverse-dynamics inner loop formulated as a cone program. We solve the resulting black-box noise optimization problem using the Separable Covariance Matrix Adaptation Evolution Strategy (Sep-CMA-ES), thereby avoiding reliance on computationally expensive and discontinuous gradients. An autoregressive scheme then chains optimized segments to synthesize long motion sequences. Across 100 motion styles on an SMPL humanoid, PhysibleMDM reduces mean ground penetration, self-collision penetration, and ground slip by 75%, 92%, and 74%, respectively, relative to unoptimized diffusion output. Across 11 sequences for a custom bipedal robot, it achieves median reductions of 89.5% in per-sequence mean acceleration-reconstruction error and 79.5% in the mean inverse-dynamics residual.

papers.title: Externalise the Memory: A Pre-Registered Study of Where an Embodied Agent's Experience Should Live
papers.abstract: Should an embodied agent's experience be baked into its policy weights, or kept external and retrieved at inference? A memory-augmented teacher (a VLM that retrieves lessons, with their episode images, from its own past attempts) produces trajectories on a vision-conditioned reach task; from the same trajectories we distil LoRA student policies and evaluate them under matched protocols, including one that re-attaches the teacher's frozen retrieval buffer to a fixed set of student weights. We pre-registered the hypotheses, arms, tests, and analysis rules before training and before any p-value. Distilling the memory-augmented behaviour into weights beat an action-only control by +1 pp (n.s.); the registered test proves underpowered for its own minimum effect, so we withdraw - rather than refute - the memory-in-weights claim. Attaching retrieval to a fixed set of student weights added +34 pp (z=5.15), reaching the pooled memory-augmented teacher reference (49.3%); the pre-registered protocol contrast agrees (+23 pp, z=3.36); under a pre-registered auto-reset sensitivity count the two are +36 and +29 pp. An exploratory behavioural probe with pre-registered per-arm predictions is consistent with behavioural distillation transferring the marginal correction but not the conditional, situation-specific correction that retrieval supplies. The recipe that follows is to externalise the memory: in follow-up controls registered before they ran, the same frozen buffer lifts the base model with no adapter to 48% (sensitivity 48%) and the other three adapters from 19-26% to 53-55% (sensitivity 17-21% to 50-55%), and the adapter adds nothing detectable once the buffer is attached. On a second, harder task, the retrieval advantage points the same direction but falls short of significance (+6 pp, 95% CI [-4.5, +16.4]); exploratory diagnostics tie the attenuation to memory coverage.

papers.title: Integrated Respiratory Sensing and Gated Control for Autonomous Needle Insertion Via CT Bore Robotic Arm
papers.abstract: Currently, CT-guided lung biopsy is a highly manual procedure requiring patient breath-holding, iterative manual needle insertions, and repeated CT confirmation scans to accurately target a tumor. Automating this process within the CT bore--without relying on manual needle placement or patient breath-holding--has the potential to reduce procedure time, patient discomfort, and radiation exposure. In this work, we present an integrated sensing and control system capable of performing a gated needle insertion within the CT bore. The experiments demonstrate the system's ability to track and predict patient breath cycles, perform autonomous respiratory-gated needle insertion, and detect breath cycle anomalies.

papers.title: Tactile-Based Robotic Manipulation: From Mechanics-Driven to Data-Driven Perspectives
papers.abstract: Tactile sensing provides robots with direct access to physical interactions at the contact interface, making it a critical modality for robust and dexterous manipulation. Over the past several decades, tactile-based manipulation research has evolved from mechanics-driven approaches, which explicitly interpret tactile signals through contact mechanics and task-specific reasoning, to data-driven approaches that learn tactile representations and manipulation policies directly from data. This paper reviews the development of tactile-based manipulation from these two complementary perspectives. We first introduce the fundamentals of tactile sensing, and then review, from a mechanics-driven perspective, how those signals form manipulation-relevant state representations and subsequently influence the robot action. We then examine the recent advances in data-driven tactile manipulation, covering imitation learning, reinforcement learning, vision-language-action models, and predictive models. Finally, we discuss open challenges and future opportunities toward scalable, generalizable, and robust tactile-enabled robotic systems.

papers.title: Integrated Longitudinal and Lateral Control for High-Speed Platooning of Articulated Vehicles
papers.abstract: This paper presents an integrated control framework for high-speed platooning of articulated vehicles, combining advanced longitudinal and lateral control strategies to address the challenges of safe and efficient autonomous driving. A novel proof of string stability for the proposed longitudinal control algorithm, based on a PID framework, ensures robust inter-vehicle distance regulation even under dynamic operating conditions. Additionally, an arc-length-based longitudinal error formulation enhances the applicability of the control system for curved roads, making it realistic for diverse driving scenarios. For lateral control, significant improvements to the clothoid-based path tracking algorithm are introduced to mitigate oscillations and enhance stability at high speeds. These enhancements include a tangential criterion for oscillation reduction, trajectory segment classification for adaptive lookahead distance tuning, a dual-adaptive mechanism for regulating the rate of lookahead distance adjustments based on both cross-track error (CTE) and anticipated road curvature, and extensions for articulated vehicle dynamics. The proposed integrated control framework is validated through simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness in maintaining stability, minimizing tracking errors, and ensuring robust performance in high-speed and challenging platooning scenarios.

papers.title: MPBRS: Multi-Potential-Based Reward Shaping for Unified Reward Configuration in Humanoid Locomotion
papers.abstract: Designing and tuning reward functions remains one of the main challenges in building effective reinforcement learning (RL) pipelines for humanoid locomotion. While shaping rewards can accelerate learning, naively formulated terms often conflict with the desired behavior, overfit to a specific robot, or become unstable under small weight changes. Potential-Based Reward Shaping (PBRS) offers an alternative solution: shaping the reward via differences of a potential function to guide exploration without changing the optimal policy. In this paper, we study Multi-PBRS for humanoid locomotion and propose a unified reward configuration. We then evaluate the same reward structure and weights across nine humanoid robots, requiring only robot-specific metadata (joint/link mappings and default poses) rather than per-robot reward redesign. Our experiments show that, compared to standard shaping, MPBRS provides more consistent scaling behavior and reduced tuning sensitivity across robots, making it easier to tune without altering the optimal policy.

papers.title: Self-Distilling Future Video Representations for World Action Models
papers.abstract: World Action Models (WAMs) have emerged as a promising approach to learning generalist robot policies using rich spatiotemporal priors from pre-trained video diffusion models. A recent line of WAMs improves inference efficiency by conditioning a separate action decoder on intermediate future video representations extracted from a single denoising step, avoiding costly iterative denoising required for video generation. This design makes action prediction depend directly on the quality of these future representations. In this paper, we introduce Future REpresentation learning via self-Distillation with temporal context (FRED), a framework that trains WAMs to improve the quality of future video representations from noise in a single denoising step. Specifically, FRED uses self-distillation to predict future representations from noise, using representations extracted from ground-truth future observations as targets. We further condition the video model on historical observations, providing temporal context for predicting future representations better. Across diverse real-world manipulation scenarios, FRED consistently outperforms competing WAMs. It achieves particularly large gains on long-horizon and out-of-domain tasks under zero-shot environment generalization, and substantially improves human-to-robot skill transfer, reaching 50.0% task success on tasks absent from robot training data and demonstrated only in human videos, compared with 19.4% for the best competing WAM.

papers.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
papers.abstract: End-to-end autonomous driving has achieved state-of-the-art performance on benchmarks and real-world deployments. Its standard training recipe, however, is expensive across all existing paradigms: imitation learning requires fleet-scale driving logs whose behavior distribution only thinly covers the safety-critical tail; closed-loop reinforcement learning in a photorealistic simulator, while offering diverse behaviors, is bottlenecked by sample-efficiency, per-step cost of rendering, and a forward pass through a large vision backbone. Self-play in vectorized simulators changes the economics: at millions of rollout steps per second, one can obtain a state distribution with natural diversity in collisions, near-misses, and recoveries that no driving log contains, and a highly reactive policy emerges from a basic driving-quality reward. Our approach exploits this asymmetry. We pretrain a single policy by self-play, distill its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher that also plans, and train lightweight adapters on a frozen pretrained vision backbone to reproduce the latent space of either teacher through the action KL divergence, a batch-relational low-rank structural loss, and, for the planner, a trajectory-matching loss. Every target traces back to the self-play policy, so alignment never supervises against a logged trajectory: a paired dataset of (image, scene-state) frames suffices, with no need for the curated expert demonstrations that imitation pretraining is built on. From this one self-play teacher we obtain two end-to-end students: a closed-loop policy that outperforms every published imitation-based end-to-end method on the photorealistic 3D Gaussian splatting closed-loop benchmark HUGSim, and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard, above every published method including DriveZero-Scale (57.1), and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, without human demonstrations.

papers.title: Alpha: Systematic Fault Injection and Robustness Evaluation for LLM-Driven Embodied Manipulation
papers.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly integrated into embodied robotic planning, yet standard benchmarks primarily evaluate end-to-end task completion in nominal environments, obscuring failure origins across the execution stack. We present Alpha, a systematic fault-injection and robustness-evaluation framework for LLM-driven manipulation in simulation. Alpha injects calibrated faults across perception (sensor lag), actuation (grip slip), kinematics (unreachable targets), and planning (planner-output corruption), alongside concurrent conditions. To separate physical vulnerabilities from planner sensitivities, we introduce a matched methodology pairing an LLM agent (Llama-3 via Ollama) against a deterministic Scripted Oracle planner across a balanced 150-episode matrix under identical seeds, geometries, and safety criteria. Across the matrix, the Oracle achieves 64.0% (48/75) success while the LLM achieves 44.0% (33/75) (paired McNemar p = 3.01 x 10^-4). Crucially, excluding planner-output corruption, performance across all physical and kinematic conditions is identical: 55.0% (33/60) for both planners with zero discordant pairs (McNemar p = 1.00). This demonstrates that physical actuator slip, kinematic reach boundaries, and perceptual staleness affect deterministic controllers and LLM planners equivalently. The performance gap is driven entirely by planner-output corruption (100% Oracle vs. 0% LLM), isolating the prompt-to-JSON serialization and validation interface rather than a cognitive reasoning deficit. We also audit 169 historical pilot attempts for transparency.

papers.title: Sensorimotor Alignment: A Platonic Proxy for Embodied Policy Success
papers.abstract: Robotic foundation models are typically evaluated through costly closed-loop rollouts, which motivates cheap offline proxies for model capability. The Platonic Representation Hypothesis (PRH) suggests that as representations improve, different modalities such as vision and language converge toward a shared statistical model of reality. We ask whether motion trajectories form another such modality: as embodied models become more capable, should their sensory representations converge toward the structure of physical motion? To examine this, we propose Sensorimotor Alignment ($S^2$), a training-free offline metric that measures how well a model's sensory representation aligns with the geometry of physical motion. We find that $S^2$ correlates positively with downstream robot task success across embodied model families, making it a low-cost offline proxy for prioritizing models before closed-loop evaluation. $S^2$ can also identify promising vision-language model (VLM) backbones even before costly fine-tuning into vision-language-action models (VLAs). Beyond this correlation, $S^2$ offers representation-level explanations for phenomena observed in VLAs and world action models (WAMs). With $S^2$, we extend PRH to embodied models and make sensorimotor alignment empirically measurable, offering insight into why an embodied model succeeds beyond its closed-loop success rate.

papers.title: Decentralized Bi-Level Optimization for Cooperative Orbital Transportation of a Rigid Payload
papers.abstract: The rapid growth of the space economy, alongside increasing orbital congestion and debris, is driving demand for reliable on-orbit transportation of large and non-cooperative objects. Performing such transportation with a swarm of small spacecraft distributes risk and removes the single point of failure inherent to monolithic architectures, but requires solving a non-convex trajectory optimization coupling every agent's cone-constrained thrust to the payload's rotational dynamics. Existing approaches span decentralized control laws with asymptotic guarantees but limited constraint enforcement, and centralized and partially centralized planners that reintroduce a single point of failure. In this work, we present a decentralized bi-level framework driven by exact gradients: the problem is split into an inner convex thrust allocation and an outer search over payload torque trajectories. This decomposition yields fuel-efficient solutions quickly, without requiring full NLP convergence, and at short timescales its performance scales with the number of agents. Theoretical convergence guarantees are established, and the method is validated through extensive Monte Carlo simulation, including closed-loop recovery from in-flight faults. These properties make the framework well suited to spacecraft swarm applications.

papers.title: PhysTrace: Interpretable Temporal Evaluation of Physical Consistency in Video Generative Models
papers.abstract: World action models increasingly rely on pretrained video models assumed to capture physical dynamics for prediction, planning, and action generation. Existing evaluations assess plausibility, probe representations, or measure predictive surprise, but rarely identify which history-conditioned physical expectations conflict with observations. We introduce PhysTrace, a training-free framework aligning MLLM-generated, history-conditioned expectations with observed video windows to temporally localize physical violations and provide interpretable descriptions without task-specific probes or classifiers. We also introduce IntPhys2-Timing, adding violation intervals to IntPhys2. PhysTrace achieves a Hit Rate of up to 70.7% across physical principles on IntPhys2-Timing and outperforms the compared methods in overall possible-impossible discrimination accuracy on IntPhys2. Applied to reconstructed videos along the trajectories of pretrained diffusion/flow-based video models, PhysTrace reveals attribute- and noise-dependent patterns in physical violation localization, enabling interpretable physical consistency analysis across timesteps.

papers.title: Inside-JEPA: From Prediction to Relational Grounding in Latent World Models
papers.abstract: Joint-embedding predictive architectures (JEPAs) learn world models in latent space, enabling efficient planning but leaving their states opaque. We introduce Inside-JEPA, which places relational channels for ordered entity pairs inside the JEPA latent state and shows that an inverse-dynamics loss can ground these channels without relation labels when its head reads them, either alone or as part of the full state. On Something-Something V2, latent prediction alone performs no better than a random relation head, while inverse-dynamics supervision that recovers actions from channel changes improves relational AUROC by .065-.103 across ten settings with annotated boxes, by .081 on RH20T robot episodes with held-out tasks, and by .050-.061 across five relations using off-the-shelf detection and tracking. An inverse head on entity latents decodes actions more accurately but barely improves relational grounding; shuffled labels, two label-free objectives, and action labels on only 5% of the pairs also fail to ground the channels. Given an action, predicted relational changes approach the quality of observed future relations (AUROC .599 vs .621). For one-step relational goals, a supervised readout of the 16 channels ranks the correct action among the top five of 65 in 43% of cases, compared with 24% for prediction-only latents and 17% for a frequency prior.

papers.title: Navigating human-robot interaction challenges in private and residential aged care homes
papers.abstract: This chapter explores how robotic systems and ambient intelligence can enhance care for older adults in residential aged care (RAC) homes and private homes. Although these settings differ, we frame both as extreme and challenging environments for human-robot interaction (HRI), characterised by cluttered and dynamic layouts, diverse resident needs, and limited on-site technical support. We review embodied and non-embodied systems that assist with daily living, safety monitoring, and social engagement, highlighting hybrid deployments where robots complement fixed and wearable sensors. To ensure these technologies are usable and effective, design considerations consider the cognitive, physical, and social needs of older adults. Interaction design prioritises accessibility for older adults with low digital literacy, using robust but simple voice interfaces, small sets of non-verbal cues, accessible screen-based companions, and safe object handovers. Privacy, trust, and acceptability are addressed via practical strategies such as on-device inference, data minimisation, visible consent controls, and transparent data handling aligned with emerging artificial intelligence (AI) and privacy regulation. Evaluation emphasises real-world metrics including false alarms per day, time to recover from faults, staff workload, and long-term system reliability. We close by outlining open research challenges and future directions for scalable, regulation-ready deployments that support aging with dignity, safety, and independence.

papers.title: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media
papers.abstract: Legged locomotion on flowing ground ({\em e.g.} granular media) is unlike locomotion on hard ground because feet experience both solid- and fluid-like forces during surface penetration. Recent bio-inspired legged robots display speed relative to body size on hard ground comparable to high performing organisms like cockroaches but suffer significant performance loss on flowing materials like sand. In laboratory experiments we study the performance (speed) of a small (2.3 kg) six-legged robot, SandBot, as it runs on a bed of granular media (1 mm poppy seeds). For an alternating tripod gait on the granular bed, standard gait control parameters achieve speeds at best two orders of magnitude smaller than the 2 body lengths/s ($\approx 60$ cm/s) for motion on hard ground. However, empirical adjustment of these control parameters away from the hard ground settings, restores good performance, yielding top speeds of 30 cm/s. Robot speed depends sensitively on the packing fraction $\phi$ and the limb frequency $\omega$, and a dramatic transition from rotary walking to slow swimming occurs when $\phi$ becomes small enough and/or $\omega$ large enough. We propose a kinematic model of the rotary walking mode based on generic features of penetration and slip of a curved limb in granular media. The model captures the dependence of robot speed on limb frequency and the transition between walking and swimming modes but highlights the need for a deeper understanding of the physics of granular media.

affiliation_blocks.text: Sensitive dependence of the motion of a legged robot on granular media Chen Li 1 , Paul B. Umbanhowar 2 , Haldun Komsuoglu 3 , Daniel E. Koditschek 3 , Daniel I. Goldman 1 1 School of Physics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA 30332 2 Department of Mechanical Engineering, Northwestern University, Evanston, IL 60208 3 Department of Electrical and Systems Engineering, University of Pennsylvania, Philadelphia, PA 19104 Published in Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences 106(9), 3029–3034 (2009). DOI: 10.1073/pnas.0809095106 Keywords: granular media , robotics , locomotion , control Compared to agile terrestrial organisms, most man-made vehicles possess limited mobility on complex terrain [ 1 ] and are easily thwarted by materials like rubble and sand. Increased locomotive performance of engineered platforms demands better understanding of interaction with complex environments. At the same time, there is increasing evidence that small legged machines can have greater maneuverability than large wheeled vehicles in many natural environments [ 2 ] . However, while wheeled and treaded locomotion on sand has been well studied by pioneers like Bekker [ 3 ] , study of the interaction of animals or legged devices with complex media like sand is in its infancy [ 4 ] , in part because the physics of penetration and drag in granular media is largely unexplored for realistic conditions. Nearly all previous experiments and models of terrestrial locomotion were developed for running and walking on rigid, flat, non-slip substrates in which the possibility of substrate flow was ignored [ 5 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 9 ] . Rainforest, grassland, polar tundra, mountains, and desert are examples of complex Earth terrains with flowing substrates that challenge locomotors; the limited experience of the Mars Rovers supports the presumption that extraterrestrial landscapes will be even more daunting. Deserts, common in nature and occupying about 10 percent of land surface on Earth [ 10 ] , consist largely of granular media, a representative complex substrate. Granular materials, defined as collections of discrete particles, can exhibit solid-like [ 11 ] behavior below a critical yield stress [ 12 ] , while fluid-like [ 13 ] , gas-like [ 14 ] , and even glass-like [ 15 ] behaviors are possible during flow. Yet, compared to other complex materials like debris, mud, or snow, granular materials are simple enough that fundamental understanding of the collective physics can be achieved through interplay of experiment and theory. Unlike more heterogeneous real-world environments, granular media can be precisely controlled using laboratory scale devices [ 15 , 16 ] to create states of varying material strength that mimic different deformable flowing materials produced during locomotion on complex terrains. Here we systematically explore the performance of a small legged device, SandBot, on granular media prepared in different packing states with volume fraction ranges typical of desert sand [ 17 ] . Despite SandBot’s (and its predecessor RHex [ 18 ] ) ability to move nimbly and rapidly over a wide range of natural terrain, we find that on granular media the locomotion is remarkably sensitive to substrate preparation and gait characteristics, which points to both the need for a more sophisticated understanding of the physics of motion within granular media and the possibility of better robotic design and control paradigms for locomotion on complex terrains.

papers.topic_rationale: Study concerns legged locomotion physics on granular media, not navigation, manipulation, or whole-body control; extensive real-robot experiments on SandBot across gait and terrain conditions.

executive_summary: Across diverse navigation domains, new traversability-aware controllers couple richer environment modeling with risk or preference reasoning: EBV-CAN uses a static external bird’s-eye image plus evolving endoscopic views and semantic queries to localize flexible endoscope tip/waypoints and predict bending/insertion commands, achieving 97.5% tip and 94.8% waypoint localization accuracy and 76.25% success in 1,920 physical trials while exposing a gap between low offline imitation error and real-world success; PATH-Net fuses visual/geometric bird’s-eye features and short-term vehicle history with inverse reinforcement learning to produce operator-preference-conditioned off-road cost maps and speed profiles that closely match 15 users’ teleoperated paths and reduce NASA-TLX workload scores from 34.7 to 22.2; ProTrav reconstructs probabilistic elevation fields with sparse variational GPs, propagates uncertainty into traversability costs, and embeds a risk-aware UCB term in an MPPI controller to achieve >90% simulated success vs <40% for a baseline and smoother attitudes; TRACE leverages vision-language–derived confidence maps with natural-language prompts to infer traversable path boundaries and embed them as soft constraints in NMPC, demonstrating smooth autonomous navigation in cluttered forests with deformable and visually ambiguous terrain. [arXiv:2610.30786, arXiv:2610.30605, arXiv:2610.30839, arXiv:2610.30994]

New global and multi-robot planning formulations target near-optimal coordination at scale: WarpWeaver extends dispersive tree search for differentially flat systems with local constraints and decentralized column generation plus space-rent negotiations, proving that suitable local constraints can approximate joint-space optimal control and that negotiations converge to a certified near-optimal agreement, while simulations on Dynobench show up to 22% lower total travel time than centralized offline planners and up to 37% over a decentralized real-time baseline, with six-robot hardware validating onboard deployment; GlobMP casts continuous-time global motion planning and steering as a single nonconvex program over piecewise-polynomial curves, using gradient projection with alternating cost reduction and feasibility restoration to enforce polynomial inequality constraints over entire intervals and, under mild assumptions, approach globally optimal cost as the number of pieces grows, with experiments on up to 200 robots, Robotarium swarms, maze navigation, and bimanual humanoid steering showing superior performance to strong baselines. [arXiv:2610.31540, arXiv:2610.30607]

End-to-end control and monitoring methods for ground and aerial robots emphasize data-efficient training and internal representations: TerraTransfer++ trains a single self-play policy in vectorized driving simulators and distills its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher and planner, then learns lightweight adapters on a frozen vision backbone using only paired images and scene states, yielding a closed-loop policy that reportedly surpasses all published imitation-based methods on the HUGSim benchmark and a planner that reaches 59.4 EPDMS on NAVSIM navhard and 95.5 PDMS on navtest, outperforming prior state of the art without human demonstrations; ALMA learns a contextual aerial loco-manipulation flight controller that predicts future measurement representations conditioned on actions to retain responses to external arm commands, and uses an LLM-driven evolutionary process to propose harder arm motions for training, reducing simulated position RMSE by up to 24.7% versus the strongest baseline and cutting hover RMSE by 79.6% in zero-shot transfer to a real aerial manipulator; Progress Probes (P²) trains simple linear probes on internal activations of a Vision-Language-Action policy using demonstrations to estimate task progress and flag deviations, achieving task-failure detection on open-source π₀.₅ that is competitive with or better than monitors using external VLMs or failure data. [arXiv:2610.30319, arXiv:2610.30810, arXiv:2610.31613]

Several works advance sensing, mapping, and knowledge organization for manipulation and navigation: OpenTac provides a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts shear into spatially varying pressure, enabling decoding of local shear vectors from differential taxel responses and normal forces from common-mode signals, along with a full ecosystem (CAD-based design from 2D/3D outlines or text, simulator, cross-sensor transfer, fast/adaptive acquisition) that supports contact-rich control and manipulation learning and achieves kilohertz-rate partial readouts up to 19.2× faster than full-array scanning on a 1,024-taxel skin; OASIS represents scenes as sparse semantic anchors with unified multimodal states, using anchor-centric memory, on-demand evidence extraction, and hierarchical retrieval to support open-vocabulary mapping, retrieval, reasoning, and navigation while leveraging transient observations to relocalize moved objects, with experiments in simulation and real-world tasks showing robust retrieval and navigation under dynamic scene changes; CMAR-search builds Functional 3D Scene Graphs from commonsense area functionalities plus perception and memory to organize environments into functional areas and containers, enabling hierarchical macro-/micro-level planning and dynamic object relocalization, and significantly improves success rate and search efficiency over state-of-the-art baselines in large-scale dynamic object-search benchmarks. [arXiv:2610.31661, arXiv:2610.30589, arXiv:2610.30606]

Complex loco-manipulation and surgical-style tasks are addressed with new retargeting and perception-to-action pipelines: Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR) for humanoids uses a vision-language model to select key signals and body parts, identifies keyframes, and allocates extra optimization and interaction weights to preserve critical body–object relations at reduced cost, while Mechanics-Aware Contact Anchoring refines contacts via approximate wrench models and Spatiotemporal RL focuses sampling and contact-based rewards on key stages; simulations on a Unitree G1 and real-world tests on a Unitree R1 show improved geometric contact coverage/continuity and higher loco-manipulation task completion versus uniform retargeting baselines; LocoManiLab provides a unified humanoid loco-manipulation testbed with 234 tasks across five household scene types and 51.5 hours of simulated teleoperation, enabling standardized evaluation of 12 policies under shared controllers and perturbations, revealing that success drops on unseen tasks/scenes and with increased visual perturbations, and that simulation and real-world rankings of several policies align on closely matched tasks; a surgical-oriented pipeline performs live 3D reconstruction of deformable thread configurations from images while tracking past and current contact points to plan safe, optimized sequential actions for long-horizon suturing operations like needle retrieval, detangling, and knot tightening, avoiding assumptions of fixed thread pose. [arXiv:2610.30540, arXiv:2610.30876, arXiv:2610.30694]

institution_matches.title: EBV-CAN: Vision--Language Grounding for Contact-Aided Endoscope Navigation
institution_matches.overview: The paper proposes EBV-CAN, a vision-language contact-aided navigation policy that uses a single static external bird’s-eye image plus evolving endoscopic views and motor states, with supervised semantic queries to localize the tip, waypoint, and target and to predict bending and insertion commands for flexible endoscope navigation. institution_matches.title: Dispersive Tree Agreements for Multi-Robot Coordination
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces a decentralized, real-time multi-robot planner, WarpWeaver, that extends dispersive tree search for differentially flat systems and uses local constraints plus decentralized column generation with space-rent negotiations to approximate joint-space optimal control as an anytime process. institution_matches.title: TerraTransfer++: Demonstration-Free End-to-End Planner
institution_matches.overview: The paper presents TerraTransfer++, a demonstration-free end-to-end autonomous driving framework that first trains a single policy via high-throughput self-play in vectorized simulators, then distills its rollouts into a flow-matching trajectory teacher and a planner, and finally trains lightweight adapters on a frozen vision backbone using only paired (image, scene-state) frames without expert driving demonstrations. institution_matches.title: OpenTac: An Open Ecosystem for Customizable, Scalable, and Transferable 3D Tactile Sensing
institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces OpenTac, a scalable resistive tactile skin with a structured deformable overlay that converts tangential loading into spatially varying pressure, enabling decoding of local shear vectors from differential taxel responses and normal force from common-mode responses. institution_matches.overview: The paper introduces Progress Probes (P²), a lightweight runtime monitoring approach for Vision-Language-Action models that trains linear probes on internal policy activations from demonstrations to estimate task progress and flag executions that deviate from expected progress, without relying on external foundation models. topic_matches.title: Motion Retargeting with Spatiotemporal Preferences for Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
topic_matches.overview: The paper presents Spatiotemporal Retargeting (STR), a motion retargeting framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that uses a vision-language model to select key motion signals and body parts, identifies keyframes from these signals, and allocates extra optimization iterations and higher interaction weights to them to better preserve critical body–object relations at reduced computational cost. topic_matches.title: OASIS: Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System for Open-Vocabulary Retrieval and Navigation in Dynamic Environments
topic_matches.institution: Beihang University; Hangzhou Innovation Institute of Beihang University
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes OASIS, an Online Anchor-centric Scene Inference System that represents environments using a sparse set of semantic anchors, each maintaining unified multimodal representations (semantic descriptions, visual features, geometric states) to support online mapping, open-vocabulary retrieval, reasoning, and navigation in dynamic settings. topic_matches.title: PATH: Preference-Aware Traversability Estimation for Robotic Teleoperation in Off-Road Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Beijing Institute of Technology; China North Vehicle Research Institute; Hong Kong Polytechnic University
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces PATH-Net, a Preference-Aware Traversability estimation Hierarchical Network that fuses visual and geometric bird’s-eye-view features with short-term vehicle state history to generate operator-preference-conditioned traversability cost maps and speed profiles for off-road teleoperation. PATH-Net uses maximum entropy inverse reinforcement learning with sparse speed supervision and an asymmetric feature aggregation mechanism that separates a risk-focused cost branch from a preference-adjusted speed branch, enabling alignment with different operator risk and speed preferences. In experiments with 15 operators over 225 teleoperated trajectories, PATH-Net’s recommendations achieve modified Hausdorff distances of 0.17 m (aggressive) and 0.15 m (conservative) relative to user trajectories, and questionnaire results show reduced subjective workload, with NASA-TLX scores dropping from 34.7 to 22.2 when using PATH-Net recommendations.

topic_matches.title: Continuous-Time Motion Planning and Steering with Global Convergence
topic_matches.overview: The paper introduces GlobMP, a continuous-time Global Motion Planning method that formulates planning and steering as a single nonconvex program over piecewise-polynomial curves, using gradient projection with alternating cost reduction and feasibility restoration to enforce that polynomial inequality constraints hold over entire motion intervals while keeping trajectories close to learned proposals. Under mild assumptions and starting from a sufficiently fine grid, GlobMP is proven to have cost that approaches the global optimum as the number of polynomial pieces increases, while satisfying all constraints to arbitrary tolerance or exactly on stable instances. topic_matches.title: Adaptive Aerial Loco-Manipulation Policy Learning via LLM-Assisted Proactive Task Generation
topic_matches.institution: Nanjing University; National Key Laboratory of Novel Software Technology, Nanjing University; Northeastern University

topic_matches.title: ProTrav: Probabilistic Traversability with Elevation Uncertainty Propagation for Risk-aware Off-road Navigation
topic_matches.institution: Tampere University; University of Tartu; Volvo Autonomous Solutions
topic_matches.overview: The paper proposes ProTrav, a probabilistic traversability estimation framework that uses a Sparse Variational Gaussian Process to reconstruct a probabilistic elevation field, then performs posterior function-space sampling to generate spatially correlated terrain realizations and propagate elevation uncertainty through geometric features into a distribution over traversability cost at arbitrary locations.
